title: One in five fears AI redundancy
full_text:
White-collar workers are sounding the alarm about artificial intelligence, with more than one in five fearing AI could make their job redundant in three years, and 44 per cent concerned their jobs could be lost in the next decade.
Workers on the frontline of AI adoption including administrative and clerical workers and call centre, legal, and information technology employees were questioned about their attitudes to AI and how they had shifted since a similar survey 12 months earlier.
The latest Australian Services Union survey found 51.3 per cent of workers expected AI to change their role significantly, up from 39.9 per cent a year earlier.
While AI use at work had increased from 73 per cent in 2025 to 78.5 per cent now, only 32.5 per cent of workplaces offered any form of AI training, while consultation about its use at work was just 33.2 per cent.
The number of ASU members who had never used AI decreased from 27.2 per cent to 19.7 per cent across the 12-month period.
Forty-three per cent either agreed or strongly agreed that AI could make their job redundant in 10 years, with 22.5 per cent saying they either agreed or strongly agreed it would do so in three years.
When asked their opinions on redundancies due to AI, 73.7 per cent of members strongly agreed that workers should receive at least six months’ notice if they lost their job to AI.
However, there were some positive impacts of AI. When given a selection of the potential effects of AI on their work over the past 12 months, the most common answer was being freed up for other work (21.4 per cent). The second most common was workloads being more manageable (17.9 per cent).
The ASU renewed its call for employers to be required to provide six months’ paid notice to workers who lost their jobs due to AI and for companies to give two months’ notice of shift rostering changes.
ASU national secretary Emeline Gaske said AI was placing more demands on workers but nowhere near enough resources were being dedicated to ensuring that they were being trained and supported.
“While tech-bro billionaires in Silicon Valley jostle for more profits off the back of our land, water, work and natural resources, we’re calling for workers to get their fair share,” Ms Gaske said. “It was workers who built the outputs that AI is being trained on, and it’s workers who deserve to benefit from any potential productivity gains, not the CEOs reliant on their labour.
